newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia parties edge closer to alliance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia parties edge closer to alliance.

text.p: An alliance between Cambodia's royalist FUNCINPEC party and the opposition Khmer Nation Party, which is yet to be officially recognised, has moved a step closer, officials from both parties said on Saturday.

FUNCINPEC rules the country in coalition with the formerly communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP), an arrangement which has come under increasing strain since a FUNCINPEC threat to withdraw from government earlier this year.
A five-member FUNCINPEC delegation to the KNP's annual congress on Saturday was "a sign that things are moving towards a (new) coalition," said FUNCINPEC deputy Ahmad Yahya.
"The FUNCINPEC president and FUNCINPEC fully supports the KNP in the next election," said Yahya, adding that he expected the alliance to form in 1997.
According to a senior KNP official, the two parties had begun meeting to discuss an "alliance of hearts and minds".
"FUNCINPEC have realised that this unnatural coalition of democrats and former communists ... doesn't work," said the official.

Disputes over power-sharing within the country's unusual "two-headed" government came to a head in March this year when co-premier Hun Sen of the CPP warned that he would use force to block a FUNCINPEC threat to dissolve the government.
The KNP, which was formed in November last year by Sam Rainsy, an outspoken government critic, and now boasts 200,000 members, is regarded as a serious political player, some analysts say.

However, a senior aide to Hun Sen told Reuters on Saturday that the CPP was unconcerned about the imminent alliance and was confident that the party could win power alone in the next elections, scheduled for 1998.
The CPP official declined to comment on the status of the government should FUNCINPEC join forces with the KNP. "They have the right and the freedom to form an alliance," he said.
